title: Maximize Palindrome Length From Subsequences
statement:
Build a string by taking a **non-empty** subsequence of `word1` and appending a **non-empty** subsequence of `word2` to it. Return the greatest length such a string can have while being a palindrome (equal to its own reverse), or `0` if every possible choice fails to be a palindrome.

A subsequence keeps any subset of a string's characters (all of them is allowed) in their original relative order.
constraints: word1 and word2 contain only lowercase English letters
notes:
## Intuition

Without the "non-empty" rules this is the classic longest palindromic subsequence of `s = word1 + word2`, solved by interval DP: `dp[i][j]` is the longest palindromic subsequence inside `s[i..j]`. The rules only add one demand: the palindrome must use at least one character from each word. A palindrome's first and last characters are equal, so it is enough to make its **outermost pair** straddle the split: the left end in `word1` and the right end in `word2`. Every time the DP matches `s[i] === s[j]` with `i` in `word1` and `j` in `word2`, the value `dp[i][j]` is a valid candidate.

(A brute force fixes each matching pair `word1[a]`, `word2[b]` and solves a fresh palindrome problem between them, which repeats a lot of work.)

## Approach

1. Join the words into `s`, of length `n`; indexes below `split = word1.length` belong to `word1`.
2. Fill `dp` for `i` from `n - 1` down to `0` and `j` from `i + 1` up, so the shorter intervals `[i + 1, j - 1]`, `[i + 1, j]` and `[i, j - 1]` are ready. A single character gives `dp[i][i] = 1`.
3. If `s[i] === s[j]`, wrap the inner answer: `dp[i][j] = dp[i + 1][j - 1] + 2`. When `i < split <= j`, this palindrome starts in `word1` and ends in `word2`, so update `best`.
4. Otherwise drop one end: `dp[i][j] = max(dp[i + 1][j], dp[i][j - 1])`.
5. Return `best`, which stays `0` if no character of `word1` matches one of `word2`.

## Example 1, step by step

`s = "cacbcbba"` with `split = 4`. For `i = 1` (`'a'` in `word1`) and `j = 7` (`'a'` in `word2`) the characters match, and `dp[2][6] = 3` (`"cbcbb"` holds `"bcb"`), so `dp[1][7] = 5` and `best = 5`: the palindrome `"abcba"`. Other straddling matches are shorter, such as `dp[0][4] = 3` for `"cac"`, so the answer is `5`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n²) with `n = word1.length + word2.length`: each interval is filled once in O(1).
- Space: O(n²) for `dp` (two rows would also do, since row `i` only reads row `i + 1`).

## Pitfalls

- Returning `dp[0][n - 1]` is wrong: `word1 = "abacaba", word2 = "d"` has a palindrome of length 7, but it takes nothing from `word2`, so the answer is `0`.
- Only update `best` in the matching branch; a value inherited through `max` may not use `s[i]` and `s[j]` as its ends.
- When `j = i + 1`, `dp[i + 1][j - 1]` is an empty interval, which must read as `0`.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `s`, `n` | the two words joined, and its length |
| `split` | first index of `s` that belongs to `word2` |
| `dp[i][j]` | longest palindromic subsequence of `s[i..j]` |
| `best` | longest palindrome found whose ends straddle the split |
| `i`, `j` | left and right ends of the current interval |

narration.2: Treat both words as one string; any palindrome we want is a subsequence of it.
narration.4: Indexes before split come from word1, the rest from word2.
narration.5: dp[i][j] will hold the longest palindromic subsequence of s[i..j].
narration.6: Best palindrome found so far that uses both words.
narration.8: Go from the right so every shorter interval starting at i + 1 is already known.
narration.9: A single character is a palindrome of length 1.
narration.10: Grow the interval to the right one character at a time.
narration.11: Equal ends can wrap the best palindrome strictly inside them.
narration.12: Two more characters around the inner answer.
narration.13: The left end is in word1 and the right end in word2, so both subsequences are non-empty.
narration.14: This palindrome is valid for the problem: keep it if it is the longest.
narration.17: Different ends cannot both be used; drop whichever one helps less.
narration.21: The longest palindrome whose outer pair straddles the two words, or 0.
